## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Udapānadūsakajātaka* (Ja 271) is a narrative belonging to the Jātaka section of the Pali canon [Catalog; SuttaCentral]. Its framing verse opens with the words *Araññakassa isino* [Fausböll 1879]. According to the narrative framework, the Buddha related this story while residing at Isipatana, occasioned by a jackal that contaminated the monastic community's drinking-water well with excrement and urine [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1879].

After novices pelted the jackal with clods of earth to drive it away, the monks discussed the incident in the Dhamma hall [Fausböll 1879]. The Buddha informed them that this was not the first time the jackal had defiled a well, recounting a past life set at Isipatana in Bārāṇasī [Fausböll 1879]. In the story's resolution (*samodhāna*), the Buddha revealed that the jackal of that time was the same jackal, while he himself had been the spiritual teacher (*gaṇasatthā*) [Fausböll 1879].

SuttaCentral registers four modern translations across four languages and lists no curated cross-corpus parallels [SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus detects text reuse exclusively within the Pali tradition, sharing six matching segments (totaling 526 characters) with the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (Dutiyo bhāgo), while finding no cross-language alignments meeting the score threshold [DharmaNexus].
